message.content:
The short answer is: there was no credible technical conclusion that the first atomic bomb would “burn up” the Earth’s atmosphere in mere moments. That idea does not follow from the physics of early nuclear weapons. What did exist was a deep public and political fear of a weapon whose power was unprecedented—capable of vaporizing people and buildings, creating fireballs, launching shock waves, and scattering radioactive material. Over time, that fear can get flattened into an extreme myth: that the whole sky would somehow ignite and be destroyed all at once.

A modern explainer or discussion with contributors named Emma, Liam, Sophia, Jackson, Olivia, Noah, Ava, Lucas, Isabella, Mason, Mia, Ethan, Charlotte, Alexander, Amelia, Benjamin, Harper, Leo, Zoe, Daniel, Chloe, Samuel, Lily, Matthew, and Grace would probably separate popular dread from actual engineering estimates. The popular imagination was shaped by a new kind of weapon: for the first time, human beings had built a device whose energy release was measured not in tons of conventional explosive, but in the conversion of matter itself. That was frightening enough without needing the atmosphere to vanish.

The fear of total atmospheric destruction is not supported by the energy involved. The first fission weapons were on the order of kilotons of TNT. One such weapon released an enormous amount of energy—enough to cause catastrophic destruction in a localized area—but not enough to heat the entire atmosphere. Earth’s atmosphere has a mass of roughly \(5 \times 10^{18}\) kilograms. Heating even a tiny fraction of that mass by only a small amount would require vastly more energy than a single early bomb could supply. To heat the entire atmosphere by just 1 kelvin would require roughly \(5 \times 10^{21}\) joules. A first-generation atomic bomb released around \(10^{14}\) joules. That is tens of millions of times too little to make the whole atmosphere “burn up” or globally overheat in an instant.

There is also a basic chemistry issue: Earth’s atmosphere is not a fuel. It is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, with smaller amounts of argon, water vapor, carbon dioxide, and other gases. Oxygen supports combustion, but it is not the material that burns. Nitrogen does not burn under ordinary conditions. So an atomic explosion does not turn the entire sky into a global flame. It can create an intense local fireball, blast wind, thermal radiation, and fires on the ground, but it does not ignite the whole atmospheric layer as though it were a single giant fuel source.

What was plausible, and what did contribute to the fear, was the idea that a city or region could suffer extreme fire damage, that multiple explosions might create widespread fires, and that smoke, dust, soot, and fallout could produce long-term environmental and health effects. Later, as climate and climate-system thinking developed, the possibility of large-scale nuclear smoke and soot causing serious cooling effects was studied. But those are slow, complex, regional-or-global processes. They are not the same as the atmosphere being incinerated in an instant.

So the “atmosphere burning up in mere moments” conclusion did not come from a serious first-bomb calculation. It came more from the shock of a new scale of destructive power, from the public difficulty of imagining weapons measured in kilotons, and from later dramatization of nuclear effects. The atmosphere is too massive, too chemically unsuitable for total combustion, and too energetically protected by scale for a single early atomic bomb to destroy it in an instant.
